STANCE: for
STATEMENT: On my previous team I ran Lintwise for six months. It caught genuine bugs—null dereferences, dead code masked by unused imports—that reviewers miss. The quality win is real. My concern is CI cost: it added about four minutes per run. We sit at eleven-minute builds; four more pushes us toward fifteen, which feels sluggish for a twenty-person monorepo. I support requiring it, but let's run a two-week branch trial to measure the true delta first. If it holds under three minutes, green light as-is.
TLDR: Lintwise's bug-catching value outweighs cost, but the four-minute CI hit is real—trial before locking in.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: I own the pipeline, and eleven minutes is already tight for twenty developers on one monorepo. Once queue depth exceeds our runner pool, developers wait on checkout instead of feedback. Four serial minutes isn't just four—it's multiplied across concurrent PRs. Before I back this, I need two answers: Can Lintwise run as a parallel job alongside the build step, or must it be appended serially? Does it need a separate container image or extra setup? Those determine whether the real delta is four minutes or closer to one. Priya's trial is right, but scope it to parallel-capable config, not just serial insertion. I won't veto adoption—I won't approve it until we've sized queue impact under peak load.
TLDR: Undecided on serial integration. Key question is parallel execution and container reuse. Two-week trial must measure parallel config. Will block approval until peak-load queue impact is quantified.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I'm in favor, but my support hinges on one question: does Lintwise scan for committed secrets—API keys, tokens, hardcoded credentials—and flag dependencies with known CVEs or problematic licenses? If it does, making it a pre-merge gate closes a gap that's been open since this monorepo started. I've seen three near-misses this quarter where a key almost shipped in a PR. Catching that before merge, not in a post-deploy audit, is the whole point. If it doesn't cover those areas, this is a style-linter mandate, not a security control, and I'd rather we gate on a tool that actually reduces exposure. Marcus's parallel-job question matters to me too: a serial four-minute block will tempt people to request exceptions, and exceptions are where secrets slip through. Scope the trial to confirm secret-detection coverage and parallel execution, then I'm a clear yes.
TLDR: Support the gate only if Lintwise catches secrets and vulnerable dependencies; otherwise it's cosmetic. Ensure parallel execution to avoid exception-request culture that undermines security enforcement.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I ran Lintwise on a side-project React app, and it did catch real issues—unused imports, a few null-deref paths in event handlers, inconsistent prop validation. That's useful. But out-of-the-box it was noisy on JSX fragments and modern optional-chaining patterns; I spent two evenings tuning the ruleset before it stopped yelling at valid code. In a twenty-person monorepo, that tuning burden multiplies. My concern: if we flip the switch today without a tuned baseline for our JS and TS files, people will see a wall of red on every PR, ignore it, and we've just added a rubber-stamp gate. I want a two-week trial where we measure false-positive rate on actual frontend PRs, not synthetic test fixtures. I'll also watch Marcus's parallel-job numbers—on my side project it ran serially and added about three and a half minutes, which lines up with Priya's estimate. If we can get config right before making it required, I'm a yes.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: I maintain Python and SQL pipelines, so I can't speak to Lintwise on React or TypeScript. What I can say: my domain's real risks are schema drift, implicit type coercion in joins, and raw SQL that bypasses our parameterized-query helpers. Before I back this gate, I need to see Lintwise actually parse SQL files—`.sql` as a first-class target, not just string-embedded queries in Python—and flag things like unparameterized WHERE clauses or dropped null-guards in transformations. If it only handles Python imports and indentation, it's a cosmetic addition to my diffs. I also worry about serial CI: my nightly ETL jobs already eat eight minutes of the eleven; a lint pass I can't parallelize or skip for docs-only SQL PRs pushes queue times up for everyone. I'll defer until I can run it on two representative pipeline repos.
TLDR: Sana hasn't used Lintwise on her Python/SQL stack. She'll support it only if it genuinely handles SQL (unparameterized queries, schema-drift catches) and respects parallel CI so already-slow ETL jobs aren't further delayed. Wants two test repos before voting.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: As QA lead, my core worry is signal erosion. If Lintwise floods PRs with style noise—Tom's JSX false positives, Sana's unsupported SQL—engineers skim the whole CI report, including real test failures. That's a QA nightmare. The docs describe baseline-mode snapshots and per-rule severity overrides, promising suppression of known noise. I need the two-week trial to measure new-versus-pre-existing violations and run advisory-only for one sprint, blocking solely on severity-critical rules (null-deref, secrets, dependency CVEs). I also want Marcus's parallel config confirmed before gating. If the gate stays sharp and low-noise, it catches bugs my integration suite misses. Otherwise it dilutes test signal. Conditional yes, pending tuned baseline and severity-tiered enforcement.
TLDR: Conditional yes—support the gate only if the trial enforces advisory-mode for sprint one, suppresses pre-existing issues via a baseline snapshot, and blocks merges solely on high-severity findings (null-derefs, leaked secrets, dependency CVEs), so lint noise never drowns actual test-failure signal.

STANCE: for

STATEMENT: As merge-policy owner, I'll adopt the gate—but not as a flat binary check. My requirement mirrors Lars: severity-tiered enforcement. Block merges only on critical-severity findings (null-deref, leaked secrets, known-CVE dependencies). Everything else is advisory warnings that don't block. That protects merge speed for routine PRs while keeping the consistency guarantee Elena and Priya want.

Operational preconditions before I flip the switch: Marcus's parallel-job config must show peak-load CI stays under fifteen minutes total. Tom's tuned baseline must run against our actual monorepo JS/TS, SQL, and Python files—two-week trial, real PRs, false-positive rate below five percent. Sana gets her SQL-rule validation. Lars gets his severity-override dashboard live before week one.

One-week advisory sprint, then required on critical-only. I'll own exception policy: three exceptions per developer per quarter before mandatory ruleset review.

TLDR: For the gate, but scoped to critical-severity-only blocking after a tuned two-week trial on real monorepo PRs. Parallel CI config (Marcus), false-positive threshold under 5% (Tom), SQL coverage (Sana), and a severity-override dashboard (Lars) are hard preconditions. One advisory sprint, then enforce on null-deref, secrets, and CVEs. I own the exception ledger.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: As someone still learning our conventions, I honestly want a tool that tells me what "good" looks like instead of guessing from PR comments. But Tom's description of a wall of red terrified me—if I push a PR and see forty violations, half of them false positives from modern syntax I'm learning, I won't know which to fix and which to ignore. Jin's severity-tiered plan is what I need: critical-only blocking means I won't stall a teammate's merge over a missing JSDoc comment. I'm asking for one thing beyond the trial: a one-page style guide that lists which rules actually block, written for someone new. One week of advisory mode feels short for me. Two, matching the trial, would let me learn the ruleset before it can block my PRs.
TLDR: None

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I used Lintwise daily for six months on a prior backend-heavy team. It caught real bugs—race conditions in async handlers, SQL-injection patterns, missing null guards on deserialized payloads. But it consistently added four minutes per pipeline. With our eleven-minute builds, that's a 36 percent jump; Marcus's queue-contention concern is legitimate. My vote is yes, contingent on the trial: tuned ruleset first, parallel execution to claw back CI time, and one-sprint advisory mode before enforcement. I can own backend-ruleset tuning—I know which defaults produce noise on Go and Python. Two weeks on real PRs and I'll deliver a baseline under five percent false positives.
TLDR: Prior Lintwise user; four-minute CI hit is real but bugs were too. Conditional yes pending tuned ruleset, parallel execution, advisory sprint, and sub-5 percent false-positive baseline. I'll handle backend config.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: I own the pipeline, so I'll speak to numbers. Eleven minutes becomes fifteen with a serial Lintwise step—roughly 36% queue-time increase across twenty developers. At peak merge windows we already queue four-to-five PRs; add four minutes per slot and that queue doubles. I need Marcus's parallel execution confirmed: container reuse, lint job sharing the build cache, and a hard wall-clock cap so a misbehaving lint job can't consume a runner. Ravi's four-minute and Tom's three-and-a-half figures don't account for cold-start container pulls on our ephemeral runners. Two-week trial is right. Measure queue depth at merge-window peaks, not average wall-clock. If parallelization keeps added time under ninety seconds and queue stays flat, I'm a yes. Otherwise I'll object on pipeline-stability grounds.
TLDR: CI owner requires parallel execution, cache reuse, and a wall-clock cap on the lint job before approval. Trial must measure peak queue depth, not average runtime. Sub-ninety-second addition with flat queue means yes; otherwise she'll block on stability grounds.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I back the gate, but only if the blocking set is explicitly our security rules: hardcoded credentials, tokens in config files, dependency CVEs at CVSS 7+, and unparameterized SQL (Sana flagged this, and it's my top DB risk). Cosmetic lint rules belong in advisory mode—full stop. Elena's concern about an exception-request culture is mine too: if a junior dev can "waive" a secret-leak warning to unblock a sprint merge, we've built a security theater. Jin's severity-override dashboard must route security findings to a separate, logged exception path I co-own, not the same queue as style nits. On tuning: Tom's false-positive worry applies to security rules differently. A missed real secret is catastrophic; one false-positive "possible key" string costs thirty seconds of review. I'll tolerate higher noise on the security tier. For the trial, I want a deliberate seeded-secret canary in two test repos to validate detection coverage before enforcement.
TLDR: None

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I ran Lintwise on my React side project—Tom's tuning pain is my daily reality. Modern JSX patterns, optional chaining, and conditional rendering tripped false positives everywhere. In a twenty-person monorepo where I review most frontend PRs, that noise becomes a rubber-stamp gate fast. I support the severity-tiered approach: block only on secrets, null-derefs, and CVEs at CVSS 7+; cosmetic JS rules stay advisory. For the trial, I'll help tune the frontend ruleset against real PRs so Olga and newer devs get actionable messages, not forty red lines. Two-week advisory sprint on my files before enforcement, then I'm on board.
TLDR: Supports the gate with severity-tiered blocking. Frontend-specific tuning on real PRs is non-negotiable before enforcement; will co-own the JS/TS ruleset so new devs aren't buried in false-positive noise.

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: I haven't touched Lintwise, so I can't speak to its Python and SQL depth from experience. Sana raised the right concerns for my stack: does it flag unparameterized queries, detect schema-drift risks, or respect noqa-style suppressions we already use in pipeline scripts? I need to run it on two real pipeline repos—my nightly ETL DAG and the ad-hoc reporting queries—before I'd vote yes. On CI: Mei's wall-clock cap matters most to me because my Spark-submit stages already dominate the eleven-minute build; a lint job that queues serially behind container pulls will push a pipeline PR from eleven to fifteen minutes and make teammates skip re-runs. I support Jin's severity-tiered plan and agree with Noah that unparameterized SQL belongs in the blocking set, not advisory. My ask: give me the trial repos with my exact Airflow and dbt config so I measure SQL-rule precision, not synthetic fixtures. If it catches a real injection risk in my code without a fifty-rule ruleset rewrite, I'm in. Otherwise it's another linter we configure for a sprint and forget by the next one.
TLDR: Undecided pending hands-on trial on my Python/SQL pipeline repos. Need proof it catches unparameterized SQL and schema drift without a ruleset rewrite, and confirmation that CI parallelism keeps my ETL jobs within Mei's wall-clock cap. Backs severity-tiered enforcement; unparameterized SQL should block.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I've read Lintwise's docs; it supports severity tiers and baseline-ignore, matching Lars and Jin. My concern: if lint output merges with test-failure logs, I can't triage a red pipeline in a minute. Lint must be a separate parallel job with its own pass/fail indicator. Docs confirm container-cached parallel execution, so Mei's ninety-second cap is achievable. I back critical-tier-only enforcement with baseline suppression. My addition: pair the two-week trial with a deliberately flaky test suite to measure whether lint noise degrades triage speed. If triage time holds, firm yes post-trial.
TLDR: Support enforcement post-trial provided lint runs as a parallel job with its own pass/fail signal separate from test output, blocking is critical-tier-only with baseline suppression, and a flaky-suite stress test confirms test-failure triage speed is unaffected.

STANCE: for

STATEMENT: As policy owner, I adopt this with the severity-tiered structure. Advisory mode two sprints, baseline snapshot day one, then enforce only on null-derefs, CVSS 7+ CVEs, leaked secrets, and unparameterized SQL; everything else stays advisory permanently. I'll write Olga's one-page doc by sprint one, codifying Jin's exception ledger and Noah's separate security-waiver path. Trial gates: 5% false-positive ceiling on real frontend PRs, parallel lint under ninety seconds per Mei, seeded-secret canary per Noah, triage-time check per Hana. Fail any threshold and I pull the gate. I own merge policy; I'm committing.

TLDR: Yes with the team's severity-tiered conditions. Two-sprint advisory, baseline suppress, enforce only on security and crash bugs. I own the policy doc and exception process; hard numeric thresholds decide whether the gate survives the trial.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I've never run Lintwise, so I can't judge CI timing or false-positive rates. But I can say what it's like to be the newest person here: right now, style feedback arrives as scattered PR comments, and I often can't tell which notes are must-fix and which are preference. A tool that separates "this will block your merge" from "here's a suggestion" is exactly the clarity I wish I'd had on my first week. Olga's point about not seeing forty violations with no idea which matter—that's my daily fear, honestly. So I'm for the gate, *provided* the two-week advisory window is real and the blocking list stays narrow: null-derefs, secrets, CVEs, unparameterized SQL. Everything else advisory. I also want to be on the trial cohort—not as a configurator, but as a test reader. If I, a first-month intern, can open a PR and understand within two minutes which findings I must fix, the ruleset works. If I can't, it doesn't.
TLDR: None

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: I own the pipeline. Going 11→15 minutes serially across twenty concurrent PRs is a queue nightmare I won't sign off on. The gate is fine if Lintwise runs as a parallel job with its own container, separate pass/fail signal, and aggressive caching—Mei's sub-90-second cap is the number I'd enforce. Peak queue depth, not average runtime, kills us: two devs waiting for a runner slot is a productivity cliff. Trial must be instrumented on p95 queue-depth under simulated 20-PR burst load. Validate parallel config under that load before flipping required, and give me a tuned ruleset. With that data, I'll greenlight the merge gate.
TLDR: Gate OK if parallel, cached, under 90 s. Trial must prove p95 queue depth survives 20-PR burst. No tuned ruleset, no enforcement.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I run most of our JavaScript, so a misconfigured gate hits me hardest—every false positive on a React Native lifecycle pattern or modern JS construct is a three-second interrupt I pay fifty times a day. I tried Lintwise on a side project: it caught real null-check gaps and stale dependency flags, but also flagged valid useCallback patterns and called our navigation config "magic numbers." I need the two-week advisory window, and I'm volunteering to lead JS/TS ruleset tuning so new devs aren't buried. Critical-tier-only blocking—null-derefs, secrets, CVEs, unparameterized SQL—is the right scope. The 90-second parallel-job cap matters specifically for me: mobile builds already push past twelve minutes, and I can't afford a serial lint step stacking on top. Give me a tuned ruleset, parallel execution, and baseline suppress, and I'll greenlight it.
TLDR: Support the gate as a parallel job with critical-tier-only blocking, a two-week advisory window, and baseline suppression. I'll co-lead JS/TS tuning because I write most of our JS and mobile builds are already long; the 90-second cap under parallel execution is non-negotiable before enforcement.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: As release manager, I approve the gate under the severity-tiered conditions this round converged on. Critical-tier-only blocking—null-derefs, secrets, CVEs, unparameterized SQL—keeps merge throughput intact; advisory noise must never stall a release cut. I own the policy doc Ben flagged and the exception ledger Jin proposed: security findings route through Noah's logged path, style nits stay advisory and never enter merge policy. The two-week advisory sprint is non-negotiable before enforcement. One correction: the motion says "every repository," but we maintain one monorepo. I'll revise the motion text to scope it there so scope creep can't ambush us post-adoption. If trial metrics—p95 queue depth under baseline, sub-ninety-second parallel lint, FP rate under five percent—come back green, I make it a hard gate for the next release cycle. If they don't, I pull it from policy and we revisit.
TLDR: Conditional yes tied to trial metrics. Security-tier-only blocking, two-week advisory, monorepo-scoped motion rewrite. I own merge policy and exception routing.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I ran Lintwise daily for six months on a previous team. It caught seventeen real null-derefs and two dependency CVEs before production—cost me four extra minutes per build, matching Priya and Marcus. I've seen what happens when you enforce cosmetic rules as blockers: exception fatigue, blanket waivers, security findings drowning in style noise. The severity-tiered plan everyone converged on—block only on null-derefs, secrets, CVEs, unparameterized SQL—is exactly how I wish we'd run it back then. One addition from my experience: baseline suppression is non-negotiable. We launched without it; first sprint produced three hundred findings on legacy code, morale cratered, and we lost two engineers' trust in the tool before it caught anything useful. Pin the baseline, run advisory two weeks, tune on real PRs, then flip the gate. I support the motion as scoped to our monorepo with Theo's correction. I'll co-own security-tier rules with Noah; I've configured that layer before.
TLDR: Vera backs the gate based on six months of prior Lintwise use. She endorses the severity-tiered plan (block only null-derefs, secrets, CVEs, unparameterized SQL) and stresses that skipping baseline suppression destroyed team trust on her previous rollout. She volunteers to co-own the security ruleset with Noah and wants Theo's monorepo-scoped revision locked in before the two-week advisory sprint begins.

**CHAIR — Round 2 prompt**

Thank you, everyone. The group has converged on a structure: severity-tiered blocking (null-derefs, leaked secrets, CVSS 7+ CVEs, unparameterized SQL), advisory for everything else, two-week advisory sprint on real PRs, baseline pinned day one, parallel execution with a sub-ninety-second cap, and a seeded-secret canary before enforcement. Ben and Theo are drafting the revised motion scoped to our single monorepo.

Before we move to a second round, I have a short list of **factual questions** that, if answered, close the remaining gaps. Please answer only what you know from your own experience or the Lintwise documentation you've read. No one needs to restate their vote.

1. **Secret & CVE coverage.** Elena, Noah—have either of you seen Lintwise ship a *named* rule for hardcoded-secret detection or dependency-CVE lookup, or do those require a plug-in/rule-pack we'd have to configure separately? Vera, on your prior team, was secret-scan part of the default ruleset or an add-on?

2. **SQL parsing.** Sana, Omar—does Lintwise's documentation (you've read it, Sana) describe `.sql` files as first-class parse targets with unparameterized-WHERE detection, or does it only catch SQL patterns embedded inside Python/JS strings? This is the single fact that determines whether Omar's ETL repos are testable in week one.

3. **Parallel execution on our runners.** Mei, Kofi, Marcus—do our current ephemeral runner images already include a container base compatible with Lintwise's runtime, or would we need a custom image? Have any of you previously simulated a 20-concurrent-PR burst with an added parallel job and measured p95 queue depth?

4. **Cold-start cost.** Mei mentioned cold-pull penalties unaccounted for. Has anyone measured the container-pull time for a lint-sized image on our current pool? What is the runner-pool size (number of concurrent slots)?

5. **Prior-team scale.** Priya, Ravi, Vera—how many engineers and how many repos on the teams where you saw the +4-minute figure, and was Lintwise serial or parallel there? This calibrates whether the 4-minute number transfers to our monorepo.

Please keep answers to two or three sentences. If you don't know the fact, say so and I'll assign it as a trial-week-one measurement task. After these answers we'll do a quick second round and, if the group is ready, move to a vote on the revised motion.

STATEMENT: I ran Lintwise daily for six months on a backend-heavy team; it caught three null-handling bugs in month one. But my notes cover only null-handling and CI timing—four minutes default, about one with cache. I never evaluated a secret-detection or dependency-CVE rule-pack, so I cannot confirm whether those shipped by default or needed a plug-in. Don't rely on my six months for that answer.
TLDR: none

STANCE: undecided
STATEMENT: I skimmed Lintwise's docs last week but cannot confirm .sql files are first-class parse targets. I saw Python and JS/TS listed prominently; SQL coverage appeared only as string-pattern matching inside those languages, not as native .sql parsing. I did not verify noqa-style suppressions on .sql files. Until that's confirmed, my two config-key-typo outages stay unaddressed.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: I'll stay for, but flag one gap Vera just exposed. On my six months, I saw null-handling and timing—never a secret-detection or CVE rule-pack. Elena's three near-misses and Noah's security tier depend on rules I cannot confirm exist by default. Before we lock the blocking set, someone must verify those packs ship and how to configure them; otherwise we enforce on paper and miss keys.

On timing: my notes match—four minutes default, about one with cache enabled. Hana's citation that container-cached parallel execution is documented means Mei's ninety-second cap is realistic, not aspirational. That resolves my main objection from round one.

I back Jin's severity-tiered plan: two-week advisory, baseline suppress, block only null-derefs, secrets, CVEs, unparameterized SQL. I'll co-own the Python/backend ruleset with Ravi and help validate the seeded-secret canary Noah wants.
TLDR: Priya supports the gate but warns secret-detection and CVE rules are unconfirmed in default install (Vera couldn't verify). Timing concern resolved via cache (4 min → 1 min, matching Hana's doc citation). Backs severity-tiered plan with two-week advisory, baseline suppression; will co-own Python ruleset with Ravi.

STANCE: for
STATEMENT: Hana's citation resolves my round-one blocker: container-cached parallel execution is documented, so the lint job runs alongside tests, not after them. My baseline is 6-minute peak queue wait and 11-minute builds; adding one cached minute in parallel shouldn't extend wall-clock. But I haven't run Lintwise myself—I'm still working from Priya's four-minute default. So I'm for the gate conditional on one thing I own: a 20-PR burst load test during peak queue hours, measuring p95 queue depth and total CI wall-clock. If p95 queue wait stays under 8 minutes and builds under 12, the parallel config is validated and I'll sign off. If it regresses, I block.
